newsitem.title: NEPAL: South Asia urged to act to fight spread of AIDS.
newsitem.headline: South Asia urged to act to fight spread of AIDS.

text.p: Health experts and officials from South Asia, facing an alarming growth in AIDS cases, opened a meeting on Thursday to coordinate efforts with the international community to combat the disease.
Participants attending a two-day regional meeting in the Nepali capital on HIV and AIDS will draw up a plan of action to combat AIDS in South Asia, organisers said.
"Our aim is to get on doing very pragmatic things before AIDS becomes an overwhelming problem in the region," said a spokeswoman for the Joint United Nations Programme on HIV/AIDS (UNAIDS).

UNAIDS said South Asia and Southeast Asia had 5.3 million HIV-positive people, or about 20 percent of the world's estimated number of adults infected with HIV -- the largest number after sub-Saharan Africa, which holds nearly 65 percent.
South Asia was home to six percent of the world's AIDS cases in 1994, compared to just one percent in 1993. The human immunodeficiency virus causes Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndrome.
UNAIDS is co-sponsoring the meeting with the South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation (SAARC) and the European Commission.
SAARC groups Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, the Maldives, Nepal, Pakistan and Sri Lanka, which together hold more than one-fifth of the world's population.
Experts at the conference said there was little information about sexual activity and cross-border movement in the region, which possessed "massive potential" for the spread of AIDS.

"If you can't get more specific information on sexual behaviour, then you have an uphill battle in assisting people to protect themselves," said Tim Mackay, regional programme operation manager at a United Nations regional project in New Delhi.
He said literacy levels in the region were low and many people, who did not even know how the virus was transmitted, failed to take protective measures.

There are no separate AIDS figures available for South Asia. Delegates estimated at least 2.4 million Indians are currently infected with the HIV virus. Indian government officials say nearly 53,000 cases were reported until March 31.
Delegates called for a public debate on AIDS and political commitment to fight the disease.
"This epidemic touches people very privately but also needs public debate and political mobilisation," said Edmund Appelbaum of the European Commission delegation.
